notes: Complete Commercial Court judgment on GAFTA appeal-board drafting fees under Arbitration Act 1996 s.28.

enrichment.short_title: GAFTA appeal board solicitor drafting fees reduced as disproportionate under s.28
key_facts: Agrainex Ltd (sellers) disputed GAFTA Appeal Board costs of £19,364.25 following a demurrage appeal over about $53,762.50.
Over £9,000 of the costs were legal fees charged by assistant solicitor Andrew Meads of Middleton Potts for drafting the award at £190 per hour.
The Board chairman had requested a legal draftsman during a GAFTA pilot scheme; Meads attended three days of hearings and billed about 52 hours' work.
The sellers abandoned a s.68 serious irregularity challenge and pursued only adjustment of fees under s.28 as excessive and disproportionate.
The court accepted a draftsman could be appointed in the special pilot-scheme circumstances but held Meads' fee grossly excessive for his limited drafting-only role.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under the Arbitration Act 1996 to adjust GAFTA Appeal Board fees after an abandoned s.68 challenge.
enrichment.outcome: Fees reduced to £5,000 for legal drafting (accepted by claimants as reasonable); GAFTA ordered to repay the excess; claimants ordered to pay buyers' abandoned s.68 costs, summarily assessed at £6,500.
enrichment.ratio: A competent arbitrator is ordinarily expected to draft his own reasoned award; where a tribunal appoints a legal draftsman his role is limited to recording the tribunal's findings and reasoning, not providing legal analysis under s.37, and the tribunal must scrutinise fees for fairness and proportionality to the sums and issues at stake.
legal_issues: Whether GAFTA Appeal Board fees for legal award drafting were excessive and disproportionate under s.28(2)-(3)
The proper scope and cost of appointing a legal draftsman as opposed to a lay draftsman or s.37 legal assessor
Whether a solicitor draftsman needed to attend hearings and the time reasonably required to reproduce tribunal findings

notes: Complete judgment on IAT representative notification rules; permission to appeal granted.

enrichment.short_title: Change of immigration representatives held ineffective without full rule 35 compliance
key_facts: A Somali asylum seeker dismissed by an adjudicator sought leave to appeal to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal (IAT).
Annon & Co lodged Mr Khan's grounds just within time while the Hammersmith Law Centre later sent Mr Bazini's grounds without clearly notifying a change of representative.
The IAT refused leave on Mr Khan's grounds, which alone were on the file; the Law Centre's grounds were not placed before the Vice President.
The claimant argued Annon & Co lacked authority and that the Law Centre's September letter sufficiently notified the change of representative.
The tribunal treated the matter as closed and refused review under rule 19.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of the IAT's refusal of leave to appeal and refusal to review that decision.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; tribunal entitled to treat Annon & Co as the representative and consider only Mr Khan's grounds; permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal granted; detailed assessment of claimant's costs ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where an appellant changes representative under the 2000 Rules, all three steps in rule 35(4) and (6) must be complied with—old representative and appellant must notify cessation of acting and the new representative must notify that he is acting—and non-compliance with such structural procedural requirements is not cured by an ambiguous enclosure letter.
legal_issues: Whether Annon & Co's leave application was a nullity for want of client authority
Whether the Law Centre's letter of 5 September 2002 satisfied rule 35 notification requirements
Whether the IAT had discretion under rule 18(6) to consider alternative grounds and wrongly refused review under rule 19

enrichment.short_title: Pathway project background struck from Spencer libel and contract pleadings
key_facts: Warren Spencer, a qualified lawyer and former Fujitsu/ICL in-house solicitor, brought libel and contract claims arising from his 2000 employment dispute.
The libel claim concerned alleged publications that Spencer had threatened to sabotage company contracts during a confidential HR meeting with David Sillitoe.
Spencer, acting in person, pleaded extensive background about the Pathway PFI project and alleged malice by senior management unrelated to the pleaded publications.
Miss Addy for Fujitsu applied to strike out prolix, irrelevant and vexatious pleading in both actions and to restrict disclosure.
The Court of Appeal had previously criticised irrelevant material and Spencer's willingness to make wild allegations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court applications to strike out parts of particulars of claim and for revised disclosure in overlapping libel and contract actions.
enrichment.outcome: Irrelevant Pathway project history, side-swipes and unrelated material struck out in both actions; Friend principle not applied at this stage to August publications; Spencer to serve a reduced relevant disclosure list and return Fujitsu documents.
enrichment.ratio: In defamation proceedings the issues turn on the pleaded publications and defences of justification and qualified privilege; extensive background intended to show corporate motive against unpleaded publishers is prolix, irrelevant and may be vexatious, and claimants are not entitled to turn libel trials into biographical inquiries.
legal_issues: Whether Pathway project allegations were relevant to justification, privilege or malice in the libel claim
Whether the Friend principle barred the August 2000 publications to the disciplinary investigator
Whether disclosure of unpleaded career history was permissible to establish reputation

enrichment.short_title: CCRC cannabis conviction appeal dismissed despite informant disclosure issue
key_facts: Iroegbu was convicted in 1987 of possessing about 4.4 kg of cannabis with intent to supply and sentenced to three years' imprisonment.
Police said he was found with the drugs at a flat occupied by CS; he denied knowledge and alleged police fabrication.
The CCRC referred the case after discovering CS was an informer and had recent shoplifting arrests, including six days before the appellant's arrest.
No trial application was made to exclude police interview evidence under PACE; the 1988 appeal had been dismissed.
The court ordered disclosure of a confidential CCRC annex after hearing the Crown.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal following CCRC reference against a 1987 Crown Court conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction held safe on all grounds including non-disclosure of CS's informant role and alleged PACE/Code C breaches.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to disclose that an informer had recent arrests does not render a conviction unsafe where she was not a prosecution witness and the case depended on police observations and alleged admissions; in an adversarial system a trial judge need not exclude evidence sua sponte and appellate courts will not second-guess counsel's forensic decision not to seek exclusion under s.58 or s.78 without clear grounds.
legal_issues: Whether non-disclosure of CS's informant status and subsequent prosecutions was a material irregularity
Whether incriminating interview evidence should have been excluded under PACE ss.58, 76 and 78 and Code C
Whether the trial judge's credibility comment and incomplete good-character direction rendered the conviction unsafe

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on special adjudicator direction powers following Mwanza.

enrichment.short_title: Special adjudicator could not direct Home Office interview after rule 340 refusal
key_facts: Zaier failed to attend a Home Office asylum interview and was refused under Immigration Rule 340 without merits consideration.
He had never received notification of the interview; special adjudicators repeatedly directed the Secretary of State to interview him.
Special Adjudicator Curzon Lewis allowed the appeal under rule 33(2)(a) for failure to comply with those directions without deciding asylum merits.
The IAT held the directions ultra vires and remitted the appeal for substantive determination; judicial review and this appeal followed.
By June 2001 the Home Office was ready to proceed on merits using Zaier's written statement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from Administrative Court judicial review upholding the IAT's decision on vires of special adjudicator directions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; directions to interview were substantive not procedural; Curzon Lewis had no power to allow the appeal under rule 33(2)(a) for non-compliance.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 30 directions are limited to procedural case management of the appeal before the special adjudicator; a special adjudicator has no power to direct the Secretary of State to interview or reconsider an asylum claim on its merits, and therefore cannot allow an appeal under rule 33(2)(a) for failure to comply with such directions.
legal_issues: Whether directions requiring a Home Office interview were procedural directions under rule 30
Whether rule 33(2)(a) permitted allowing an appeal without merits consideration for breach of those directions
Whether Mwanza could be distinguished where the Secretary of State had never decided the claim on merits

enrichment.short_title: Westminster lawfully terminated HDA surveying contract on one month's notice

statutes_considered.title: Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990

key_facts: Hadley Design Associates (HDA) was engaged from 1984 to survey and manage major window replacement works on Westminster's Churchill Gardens Estate.
A 1987 contract incorporated RICS 1981 Conditions, modified to allow termination on one month's notice.
In February 1996 the Council gave one month's notice terminating the contract while requiring completion of phase 4C and free rectification of supervised defects.
HDA claimed wrongful termination based on alleged collateral assurances, estoppel, implied terms and UCTA, plus additional fees after a window redesign in phase 4C.
The court found no limiting collateral contract and that fees for later stages already reflected redesign costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of wrongful termination and additional professional fees claims following contract determination.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; termination on one month's notice held valid; no implied or collateral limitation on termination; additional phase 4C fees not payable.
enrichment.ratio: Where a professional appointment expressly permits termination on one month's notice under modified RICS conditions, a party cannot imply terms or establish a collateral contract restricting termination to default, insolvency or loss of funding in the absence of proved agreement; stage-based fee entitlements crystallise at completion of each stage and later cost increases do not reopen earlier fee calculations.
legal_issues: Whether collateral conversations limited the Council's right to terminate the 1987 contract
Whether terms restricting termination should be implied as a matter of law or business efficacy
Whether UCTA 1977 s.3(2)(b)(i) rendered the termination clause unfair
Whether HDA was entitled to additional fees after phase 4C window redesign

enrichment.short_title: Shelltime 3 clause 18 final voyage includes off-hire and option periods
key_facts: Petroleo Brasileiro chartered the Kriti Akti on Shelltime 3 for 11 months plus 15 days in charterers' option, with additional clause 50 extending the charter by off-hire time.
Charterers treated the period as extended by 36 off-hire days and the 15-day option; owners refused post-expiry voyage orders at Saõ Sebastião.
The dispute turned on whether clause 18's 'period of this charter' included off-hire extensions and the option period for a final round voyage.
An arbitral tribunal held off-hire counted but the 15-day option did not, following The Aspa Maria.
Both parties appealed the preliminary issues on clause 18 construction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on questions of law under section 69 of the Arbitration Act 1996 from a GAFTA/LMAA-style charterparty arbitration.
enrichment.outcome: Charterers' appeal allowed; owners' appeal dismissed; 'period of this charter' in clause 18 means the final terminal date including basic period, clause 50 extension and option period; tribunal not bound by The Aspa Maria on this wording.
enrichment.ratio: In a Shelltime 3 charter with clause 50 off-hire extension and a clause 3 option period, clause 18's reference to 'the expiry of the period of this charter' means the final terminal date after basic period, extension period and option period combined, not the basic period alone.
legal_issues: Whether clause 50 off-hire time forms part of 'the period of this charter' in clause 18
Whether the 15 days 'more or less in charterers' option' in clause 3 is included in that period
Whether The Aspa Maria binds the construction of clause 18

enrichment.short_title: Permanent school exclusion appeal fair without investigating teachers attending
key_facts: A 16-year-old pupil (N) was permanently excluded after an alleged indecent assault on a sixth-form pupil; he said contact was accidental horseplay.
The governing body upheld permanent exclusion and the Birmingham Exclusion Appeals Panel found the charge proved on the balance of distinct probability.
Witness statements from the complainant, supporting staff and the pupil's friend P were before the panel; investigating teachers did not attend.
N's representatives argued procedural unfairness because staff who investigated the incident were not available for questioning.
The pupil had a history of prior exclusions; practical readmission was no longer possible by the time of the hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of an local education authority exclusion appeals panel decision upholding permanent exclusion.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; panel procedure held fair; no order as to costs except claimant's public funding detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: School exclusion appeals are not criminal trials; where the case against a pupil is clearly disclosed in witness statements and the pupil can present his version, fairness does not require attendance of second-hand investigating staff unless an adjournment is sought, and a panel may properly find a serious charge proved on the distinct probability standard on the evidence before it.
legal_issues: Whether the appeals panel could fairly decide the appeal without attendance of staff who investigated the incident
Whether the head teacher's belief in the cogency of the evidence improperly influenced the panel
Whether Dunraven principles required disclosure of inconsistent accounts

notes: Complete split Court of Appeal judgment on reporting restrictions in linked murder and care proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Press may name murder defendant despite younger child's care proceedings privacy
key_facts: A 7-year-old child (CS) was subject to care proceedings after his 9-year-old brother died from salt poisoning; the mother was charged with murder.
Extensive press reporting had already identified the family before criminal and family reporting restrictions were sought.
Hedley J held he could restrain publication of the defendant's and victim's identity to protect CS but declined to do so.
Section 39 orders protected CS in criminal proceedings but did not cover naming the defendant or deceased victim.
The guardian appealed for wider inherent-jurisdiction restrictions pending the murder trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from Family Division refusal to extend reporting restrictions protecting a child in care proceedings during a linked murder trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority (Lord Phillips MR and Latham LJ); Hale LJ dissenting would have allowed the appeal because Hedley J did not conduct the required Article 8/Article 10 balancing exercise.
enrichment.ratio: The High Court may in exceptional cases use its inherent jurisdiction to restrict reporting to protect a child in care proceedings, but where section 39 does not apply the court should be slow to extend restrictions beyond statutory limits; refusing to ban naming a murder defendant and victim was a permissible proportionality judgment when publicity would likely identify the child anyway and open reporting of grave criminal charges carries significant weight under Article 10.
legal_issues: Whether the inherent jurisdiction could restrain publication of a murder defendant's and victim's identity to protect a sibling in care proceedings
The proper Article 8 and Article 10 balancing exercise under the Human Rights Act
Whether the child's welfare was paramount or subject to a balancing exercise in the protective jurisdiction
The scope of section 39 of the 1933 Act in linked care and criminal proceedings

enrichment.short_title: Home Secretary lawfully deferred mandatory lifer tariff reviews pending CJA 2003

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice Bill 2003
provisions: transitional provisions for existing mandatory lifers

key_facts: Three mandatory life prisoners challenged the Home Secretary's refusal to review their tariffs after Anderson held ministerial tariff-setting incompatible with Article 6.
Cole argued his 15-year post-retrial tariff could not exceed the 11-year tariff set after his first conviction under Schedule 2 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968.
Rowland and Hawkes sought interim tariff reductions for exceptional progress in prison before new legislation.
The Secretary of State announced tariffs would be reset judicially once the Criminal Justice Bill received Royal Assent, expected November 2003.
Section 29 remained on the statute book but ministers ceased setting or reviewing tariffs except in wholly exceptional cases.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited High Court judicial review by a Divisional Court of the Home Secretary's post-Anderson tariff review policy and individual tariff decisions.
enrichment.outcome: All three applications dismissed; Cole could not rely on Schedule 2 against the Secretary of State; Rowland and Hawkes' representations lawfully deferred; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: After Anderson, any tariff setting or review by the Secretary of State under section 29 violates Article 6 because tariff-fixing is a sentencing exercise requiring an independent tribunal; Schedule 2 paragraph 2 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968 applies to courts, not the Secretary of State; pending Convention-compliant legislation the Secretary of State lawfully adopted an interim policy of deferring reviews except in wholly exceptional cases.
legal_issues: Whether Schedule 2 paragraph 2 caps a ministerial tariff after retrial at the level of the original tariff
Whether post-Anderson tariff review by the Secretary of State remains lawful
Whether deferring review until the Criminal Justice Bill unlawfully fettered discretion or relied improperly on draft legislation
Whether exceptional progress in prison must be considered before new judicial tariff-setting machinery exists
